remarks: This Offertory is used for the Feast of St. Michael 29th September. It is also used for the Feasts of St. Gabriel (24th March) and St. Raphael (24th October) without the final Alleluia, except during Paschaltide, according to the 1962 Missale Romanum. The 1961 Graduale Romanum states "sine Alleluia in Quadrag." but does not mention the omission for 24 October. The editions of the Liber Usualis from the 1950s and 1960s state "sine Alleluia" for 24 March but make no mention of the omission for 24 October.

title: Dominus vobiscum (Toni Orationum: Toni antiqui ad libitum: Tonus solemnis.)
sources: Graduale Romanum, Solesmes, 1961, p. 115*; The Liber Usualis, Solesmes, 1961, p. 100
remarks:
Hic Tonus adhibetur pro omnibus Orationibus Missae (praeter Orationem Super pópulum), sine distinctione ritus festivi vel ferialis, et in Missis Defunctorum; insuper pro omnibus Orationibus quibus praevia est monitio Flectámus génua, in quibuslibet Functionibus.
All the Prayers of the Mass (except the Prayer Super populum) may be sung in this tone without distinction as to festal or ferial rite.

title: Dominus vobiscum (Toni Orationem: Toni antiqui ad libitum: Tonus simplex.)
sources: Graduale Romanum, Solesmes, 1961, p. 118*; The Liber Usualis, Solesmes, 1961, p. 101
remarks:
This tone is used for the Prayers of the Aspersion, of the Blessings, of the Litanies, and for other Prayers of the same kind, except those which are preceded by Flectamus genua.
If this simple tone be adopted, it is used also for the Prayer Super populum. after the admonition Humiliáte cápita véstra. (as on p. 99).

title: Kyrie Orbis factor
warning: I think there are few details worth reviewing here, but I did not want to modify this by myself without submitting it to discussion. (1) Shouldn’t the text be the one of the original Fontevraud manuscript ? The Stingl Orbis Factor is already published elsewere inside GregoBase, I don’t see why the Fontevraud text had to be altered. (2) Shouldn’t the music be the one from the manuscript, and not the transcription of one particular (though beautiful) interpretation of it ? (3) The remarks section refers to an \"untexted reference line of music after the first verse\". The line of music quoted here does not belong to the Orbis Factor, it is the ending of the previous piece in the manuscript. (4) In relation to points 2 and 3 : melodies for the \"kyrie eleison\" and \"Christe eleison\" parts exists in the manuscript right after the troped Orbis Factor, but with different ligatures and with one less note for the \"kyrie eleison\" parts. Maybe those could be used instead of a simple duplication of the melodies of the Orbis Factor ?

title: Lectio libri Genesis
remarks:
This reading is based on information I have heard, about an ancient custom to sing the first lecture of Easter Vigile: supposedly, each part describing the creation day used to be sung in corresponding mode - first day in mode I, second in mode II, third in mode III and so on - until the seventh day; the canticum after the lesson continues in the mode VIII.
I was not successful in finding the information or some score of such a lesson, but I decided to try it on my own and this is the result.
Marek Klein, Easter 2020

title: Sancti venite Christi
remarks:
This hymn text is attributed to St. Sechnall (d. 457), otherwise known as St. Secundius, who was the nephew of St. Patrick. A longstanding legend states that St. Patrick and his nephew St. Sechnall heard angels singing it in the church at Dunshaughlin during the offertory before communion. From that time forward it was adopted there for use during the reception of Holy Communion. The hymn appears in the late 7th century Irish Bangor Antiphoner, which makes it perhaps the oldest known Eucharistic hymn. A popular English translation, titled “Draw Nigh and Take the Body of the Lord”, was done by J. M. Neale (1818-1866). It first appeared in his Medieval Hymns in 1851. The translation below is perhaps a bit more literal and was done by Fr. Adrian Fortescue (1874-1924). It appears in his book “Latin Hymns”, 1913.
1. Come all ye holy, take the Body of your Lord, Drink of His chalice, take the Blood for you outpoured. 2. Saved by His Body, by His sacred Blood, we raise grateful our voices unto God hymns of praise. 3. By this sacrament of the body and blood all were stripped from the infernal chasms. 4. Giver of life, He Christ our Savior, Son of God, bought our redemption by His Cross and precious Blood. 5. Dying for all men, he the Lord prepared this feast, offered as a victim, offering Himself as priest. 6. God to our fathers ordered sacrifice of old; so He in symbols Christ the victim true unfold. 7. Giver of light, the one Redeemer of our race, He to His hold servants gives abundant grace. 8. Come, who with pure hearts in the Savior’s word believe; come and partaking saving grace from Him receive. 9. God our defender, guardian sure in this our strife, gives to His faithful after death eternal life. 10. He to the hungry gives as food this heavenly bread, fountain of life, He gives to drink the blood He shed. 11. Christ, the source of all things, who here feeds us sinful men, when this great day dawns, judge of all, will come again.

title: O Cruor Sanguinis - Hildegard
remarks:
This antiphon of St Hildegard von Bingen comes from the Riesenkodex page 466va: https://hlbrm.digitale-sammlungen.hebis.de/handschriften-hlbrm/content/pageview/450567
The alignment of the melody to the text at the words "sui illa" is unclear in the MS (with 'sui' squeezed in) but it seems most likely to me to be as is transcribed here.
The remainder of the text is left incomplete without any musical notation. To complete the antiphon's melody, I have drawn from two other antiphons in the same codex:
To complete the words "illa tetigit" I have used the antiphon "O quam preciosa est" (R. 468r) where the word 'virginitas' ends with the same Sol-Fa-Re-Do sequence as on the word "suis" in this antiphon, and is followed, on the word 'virginis', by the melody used here on "illa tetigit."
To complete the remainder of the antiphon (ungue nos de languoribus nostris), I have used the first incise of the antiphon "O beatissime Ruperte" (R. 471r).
Most transcriptions of Hildegard's chant in the D mode will assume all (or most) notes on B are to be understood as B-flat. However, to avoid any assumptions, I have only included the flat signs where they are printed in the MS itself.

title: Salve Regina (solemn)
remarks:
This is an attempt to transcribe into square notation the adiastematic notation of the Salve Regina in the 11th/12th c. MS F-Pn: Lat. 2700 from Paris, pg. 001r 1.
